html:
Cassava, also called manioc, is a root crop from South America. Portuguese ships brought it to the coast of Kongo and Angola in the 1500s, part of the Columbian exchange of plants between the Americas and the rest of the world.

The crop suited Central Africa. It grows in poor soil, survives drought and locusts, and can be left in the ground for months until needed. Its leaves are eaten too. The bitter kinds hold poison and must be soaked, dried or fermented, and African cooks learned the methods, probably from Brazil.

Cassava flour fed ports like Luanda and the ships of the Atlantic slave trade. Over the next centuries it spread inland far beyond the coast. Today it is the main staple of much of Central Africa, eaten as fufu and other pastes, and Africa grows more cassava than any other continent. Maize made a similar journey to Asia in the same century.
